newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels show no signs of taking asylum bait.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels show no signs of taking asylum bait.

text.p: Peruvian rebels holding 72 hostages showed no sign on Friday of taking up Caribbean asylum offers as frustrated mediators bemoaned the lack of talks to end the 95-day-old Lima crisis peacefully.

The Dominican Republic became the second country after Cuba to offer the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas a safe haven if they free the dignitaries they are holding at the Japanese ambassador's residence.

President Leonel Fernandez accepted on Friday a request from visiting Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura to take in some of the roughly 20 rebels occupying the Japanese ambassador's home in Peru since Dec. 17.
But there was no word from rebels inside the besieged diplomatic compound following a two-and-a-half hour meeting with mediators in a Red Cross safe house across from the mansion.

And an MRTA leader in Peru's central jungle told Reuters that asylum was not up for discussion because the government had yet to consider the group's main demand of freedom for some 450 jailed comrades.

"We cannot speak about asylum when the central demand has not been yet been taken up," said a rebel leader with the nom de guerre "Comrade Alejandro," a member of the MRTA's highest policy-making body.
In Lima, meanwhile, the members of a three-man guarantors commission overseeing negotiations expressed frustration at the lack of progress in bringing the crisis to an end.

"As guarantors we have our limits. Our limit as guarantors is possibly reaching a final point," Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, the Vatican's representive on the panel, told reporters in his strongest public comments yet on the siege.

Despite such frustration at the apparent lack of progress, The New York Times reported that mediators have outlined a tentative agreement to end the crisis, whereby rebels would release the hostages and take asylum in Cuba in exchange for early parole for some comrades jailed on lesser charges.
The newspaper was quoting an unnamed diplomat close to the negotiations.
Fuelling the speculation, Cipriani confirmed on Friday the creation of a guarantors' "sub-committee" to visit jailed MRTA rebels and check on their health and conditions.
The MRTA's hostages have spent Christmas and New Year's in the mansion in the upscale San Isidro district, and indications are they will spend Easter there too.

There was was no word on when face-to-face talks between rebel chief Nestor Cerpa and government negotiator Domingo Palermo might resume. The two sides last met March 12 before negotiations were broken off in a flurry of mutual accusations.

Tokyo's envoy Komura thanked both Cuba and the Dominican Republic for their offers, but was not hopeful of a quick end. "There is still some distance between the Peruvian government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement," he told a news conference in Santo Domingo. "We should not be too optimistic."

President Alberto Fujimori on Thursday appeared to slam the door on any release of prisoners, saying Peruvians had endured too many years of guerrilla violence and too many deaths to allow any such deal.

But on Friday brought speculation the government may be ready to make some conscessions. The five-member guarantors' sub-commission paid a visit to Lima's Chorrillos women's prison to check on the condition of rebel inmates amid speculation they may be drafting a list of some who may be released.
